subject: Catching up / autumn updates & book recommendations
body:
Hi Julian,

I hope your Friday is treating you gently! I can hardly believe we are already nearing the end of September. The weather here in Burlington turned crisp almost overnight, and walking through the park this morning actually required a wool sweater for the first time this season. I've been meaning to sit down and write you a proper note ever since your quick text last month about surviving the apartment move.

Things around here have finally settled into a comfortable autumn groove. David and I took a long weekend trip up to Acadia earlier this month to catch the earliest maple leaves turning, and it was the quietest, most rejuvenating few days we’ve had all year. Aside from that, most of my spare weekends have been spent trying to rescue my vegetable garden from early frost and testing out sourdough recipes that actually rise properly in cooler room temperatures.

You had asked about reading recommendations before the summer ended, and I finally put together the list of titles that genuinely stayed with me:
- *The Overstory* by Richard Powers: You probably already read this, but if you haven't, it will completely reframe how you look at the woods behind your new place.
- *Small Things Like These* by Claire Keegan: A quiet, devastatingly beautiful novella that you can finish in an afternoon by the fire.
- *Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead* by Olga Tokarczuk: Eccentric, darkly humorous, and part philosophical mystery—definitely right up your alley.

How are you settling into the new neighborhood? Did you manage to set up your pottery studio in the garage yet, or are boxes still taking over the hallway? Absolutely no rush at all to reply to this—I know how chaotic moving into an older house can be, especially while balancing your work projects. Just take your time and drop me a line whenever your schedule opens up, even if it's weeks from now.

Sending you and Buster lots of love,

Clara

subject: Late summer hellos & a few book recommendations
body:
Hi Julian,

I hope your September is off to a peaceful start. I was out walking Barnaby along the river trail earlier this morning, watching the very first red leaves turn on the swamp maples, and you crossed my mind. It suddenly struck me that we haven't properly caught up since your trip back East in June, so I wanted to carve out half an hour with a cup of tea and send a note.

Things around here have settled into a gentle autumn rhythm. The vegetable garden went wild in August; we ended up with enough heirloom tomatoes and butternut squash to feed half of Burlington, and Mark has become slightly obsessive about canning apple chutney. On the work side, shifting to three days a week at the library archive has been wonderful. Having Thursdays and Fridays open has given me space to finally dig into watercolor painting again, even if half my attempts end up looking like abstract ink spills.

I also wanted to pass along a few book recommendations that made my summer so much richer, especially since I remember you were looking for something absorbing to read on your commutes:
- "The Light of the North" by Eleanor Finch: a really tender historical fiction set in northern Maine during the 1920s.
- "Gathering Moss" by Robin Wall Kimmerer: short, beautifully meditative essays that completely changed how I look at ordinary stones in the woods.
- "The Morning Glass": that surf memoir you mentioned ages ago—I finally picked it up at an estate sale, and you were right, it's brilliant.

How are you settling into the new neighborhood in Portland? Have you found a decent coffee spot yet, or are you still relying on your trusty Aeropress? How are Sarah and the kids doing with the start of the school year?

Please don't feel any pressure to write back right away or compose a novel in return. I know how frantic early autumn work schedules can get, so just drop a line whenever you find a quiet Sunday morning with nothing pressing on the docket.

Sending much love to you and the family,

Clara

subject: Afternoon Brief: Meridian Pay breach hits 40 retailers; Senate AI liability vote; port congestion worsens
body:
Good afternoon, Daniel.

It’s 4:02 p.m. UTC on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, and here’s what The Capitol Ledger is tracking. We’re leading with a developing story that payment operations teams should review before the end of the business day.

**1. Meridian Pay Systems breach affects at least 40 retail chains**
Meridian Pay Systems, a card-processing vendor used by mid-size retailers, disclosed this afternoon that an unauthorized actor accessed a tokenization server between August 29 and September 1. The company says customer card numbers were not stored in plaintext, but API keys and merchant identifiers may have been exposed. Visa and Mastercard have issued emergency guidance to acquirers, and the PCI Security Standards Council is expected to publish an advisory before 6:00 p.m. Eastern today. If your company uses Meridian for payment processing, the next 24 hours matter: rotate API credentials, review settlement reports for unauthorized transactions, and confirm whether your Meridian integration uses the affected tokenization endpoint.

**2. Senate advances AI Liability Act**
The Senate voted 61–38 this afternoon to advance the AI Liability Act, which would create a federal framework for damages caused by autonomous systems. A final vote is expected tomorrow, September 3. The bill includes a safe-harbor provision for companies that maintain documented risk assessments, and it would preempt a patchwork of state laws. Retail and logistics groups are lobbying for an amendment that would delay compliance until 2028.

**3. Port of Rotterdam congestion worsens**
Container dwell times at Rotterdam have risen to 7.4 days, up from 5.1 days last week, after a crane operator strike entered its fourth day. Maersk and CMA CGM have rerouted at least 12 vessels to Antwerp and Bremerhaven. The Port of Rotterdam Authority says it expects partial operations to resume by Friday, September 4, but backlogs could last into next week. If you have inbound freight through Rotterdam, check with your forwarder today.

**Quick hits**
- The FDA approved a new rapid test for respiratory syncytial virus; distribution begins September 15.
- The European Central Bank held interest rates steady at 2.75% at its meeting this morning.
- A federal judge in Texas blocked the FTC’s noncompete rule from taking effect on September 4; the case is now before the Fifth Circuit.
- The U.S. Department of Energy announced $2.1 billion for grid resilience projects; applications are due October 30.

**Your 24-hour checklist**
If you use Meridian Pay Systems, do these before 5:00 p.m. Eastern today:
1. Confirm with your IT team whether you connect to Meridian’s tokenization API.
2. Rotate all Meridian API keys and webhook secrets.
3. Pull settlement reports for August 29–September 1 and flag any transactions you don’t recognize.
4. Join the PCI Council’s live briefing at 6:00 p.m. Eastern today; registration is free at the link below.
5. Forward this brief to your security lead if you are not the right owner.

We’ll send a breaking-news update if Meridian or the PCI Council releases new guidance before 8:00 p.m. Eastern. You can read the full stories at capitolledger.com/afternoon-brief.

The agency issued a tsunami advisory for the Pacific coasts of Hokkaido and Aomori prefectures, warning of waves of up to one meter, and urged residents in coastal areas to leave beaches, harbors and river mouths and move to higher ground.

Hokkaido Railway Company suspended all local services, and the Hokkaido Shinkansen was halted between Shin-Aomori and Shin-Hakodate-Hokuto. Hokkaido Electric Power said it had begun inspections at the Tomari nuclear plant as a precaution and reported no irregularities so far; power outages were reported in parts of eastern Hokkaido. There were no immediate reports of deaths or major structural damage, and the agency said a larger tsunami was not expected, though the advisory remains in effect while sea-level readings are monitored.

subject: URGENT — Mum's in hospital, surgery tonight at 7:30 — PLEASE call me before 6
body:
Tom,

I'm so sorry to land this on you mid-project, but I need you to read this to the end and then ring me straight away. It's just gone half five as I'm writing this, and I need to hear from you before six.

Mum had a fall this morning. She slipped on the wet lino by the back door and she's broken her hip. The ambulance took her to Leeds General Infirmary — she's on Ward J28 — and she's stable, she's awake, and she's being absolutely heroic about it, but she's in a lot of pain and she's frightened. I've been here since just after ten. Claire's left work in Sheffield and is on her way up, but with the M1 as it is on a Wednesday evening she won't get here till gone eight.

Here's the part that can't wait: they want to operate tonight, at 7:30. The surgeon, a Mr Okonkwo, has been very good with her, but he says that at her age they don't like to let a broken hip sit longer than 24 hours, and because she's on the apixaban for the atrial fibrillation they've had to plan the anaesthetic and the timing very carefully. Mum can consent herself and she intends to, but when he went through the risks she got upset and started asking for you — she's asked me four times now whether anyone has rung you. The registrar needs to know by 6:00 whether the family's all agreed on the plan, and whether you're coming, because if you're on your way they may hold her slot on the list a few minutes so you can see her first. So please, step out of whatever you're in and call me before six.

There are also practical jobs today that I can't do from a hospital corridor, and Claire's stuck on the motorway too, so it may have to be you or a neighbour:

- Biscuit is shut in the utility room with food and water — she'll need letting out and a proper feed this evening, and her litter tray is in the garage so that wants moving in.
- The paramedics left the back door on the latch; someone needs to lock up properly. The spare key is still under the same plant pot, and I've texted Mrs Doherty next door but she hasn't replied.
- Mum's handbag, phone and bank cards are still on the kitchen table. Nobody has touched anything, but the house shouldn't sit unlocked with all that in it overnight.
- Her car is parked half on the pavement outside the house on Cardigan Road — it'll get a ticket or worse. Keys are in the bowl in the hall; please move it onto the drive.

I know you're up to your eyes in the Glasgow thing and I wouldn't do this if there was any way around it, but honestly, Tom, get the train if you possibly can. If you make the 6:15 from Glasgow Central you'd be into Leeds around half nine and she'll still be in recovery. If you absolutely can't come tonight, I will hold the fort and you must not feel guilty — but ring me first either way so I know what to tell the ward.

Try not to panic. The doctors keep saying this is a very fixable break and she's in good hands — she was already chatting up the male nurse earlier, which is how you know she's herself. I just want her to see your face before they take her down, and so does she.

Ring my mobile the second you've read this — before 6:00 at the very latest. Don't text, just call, and leave your ringer on after, because I may need you to talk to the ward directly.

All my love,
Rachel

subject: Eleven weeks late: the promised catch-up (house, dog, children)
body:
Dear Priya and Kevin,

At the end of June you wrote, among many kinder things:

> "Send pictures when you can, and tell Tomás congratulations from us."

It is now the middle of September, so this reply is exactly eleven weeks late, which is impressive even by my standards. In my defence, the summer swallowed us whole. But today it is Sunday, it is raining properly for the first time in weeks, both children are back at school, and I have a cup of tea and a quiet afternoon, so here I finally am.

We've been in the Kingsdown house three months now and it has mostly stopped feeling like someone else's house. The previous owners left us a fierce orange floral wallpaper in the hallway, which came off in satisfying strips over the August bank holiday, and a fig tree at the bottom of the garden, which we are keeping forever. There was a small disaster with the kitchen ceiling in July (a slow leak, now fixed, and the plumber was lovely about it), and Neil has become mildly obsessional about the chimney, but on the whole the place feels like ours. We got Biscuit at the end of July from the rescue out at Chew Magna — a lurcher of indeterminate age with enormous ears — and she has annexed the good sofa. The allotment produced roughly nine hundred courgettes, per tradition, and the beans have gone completely feral.

The children went back on the second: Tomás has started Year 7 at the big school up the road and is working very hard at looking unperturbed by all of it, and Nina is in Year 4 and has decided, this week at least, to become either an ornithologist or a bus driver. My dad had his hip replaced in the middle of July and is already back to walking the towpath most mornings, which the physio says is ridiculous and brilliant in equal measure. My mum has redirected all of her energy into the garden and now holds strong opinions about our fig tree. As for me, I'm still at the library service three days a week on the new rota at the Central Library, and I've started a Tuesday evening ceramics class where I have so far produced one lopsided bowl and one quite nice mug.

So, in no particular order, the things I want to know:

1. How did the allotment open day in August go? Did the marrow competition survive the rain?
2. Kevin — how is the knee holding up, and is the half-marathon in October still on? I want to hear that it is.
3. Did your mum ever settle into the Marchmont flat, and is she speaking to the removal men again?
4. And is there any truth to what your brother kept hinting at on that group chat, or shall I ignore him as usual?

Photos of the house, the dog, the lopsided bowl and the children will come in a separate email once I've wrestled them off my phone — I have about four hundred of the dog alone, so consider yourselves warned.

And finally: half-term here is the week of the 26th of October. If you fancied a weekend in Bristol around then, the sofa bed is made up and you'd be more than welcome — we could walk the harbour and eat our body weight in chips. Or if that's a stretch, we could meet somewhere halfway and do the same thing. Genuinely no pressure, and absolutely no rush to reply; I know September is a mad month for you both. Whenever you get round to this is fine by me, as long as you eventually do.

All my love,
Marta

Nordhaven Energy Brief — Issue 214
Thursday 3 September 2026

Dear Marcus,

Nordic hydro conditions dominated the week once again, and the effect on forward curves is now visible well beyond the Nordics. Reservoir levels across Norway and Sweden stood at 68.4% of capacity on Monday, down from 74.1% at the same point last year, with the shortfall concentrated in the south-west price areas (NO2 and NO5). Spot prices in those zones have traded at a persistent premium to the system price since mid-August, and the September front-week contract closed yesterday at €58.90/MWh against €44.10/MWh for the system. Traders we spoke to in Oslo and Bergen describe the market as "weather-driven and thin" — a phrase that has appeared in three separate broker notes this week.

The wider picture is softer. TTF front-month settled at €34.85/MWh on Wednesday, down 6.2% week on week, after a string of mild revisions to ten-day temperature forecasts for north-west Europe. EU gas storage is 89.2% full, comfortably ahead of the five-year average of 84.6%, and Norwegian pipeline nominations to the continent have held above 320 mcm/day for eleven consecutive days. German baseload front-month closed at €87.50/MWh, French baseload at €79.20/MWh, and the UK NBP front-month at 78.4p/therm. EUA December carbon settled at €71.30/t, its lowest close since 14 July.

Key numbers for the week ending 2 September 2026:

Dear colleagues,

The revised Tallowwood Group Employee Handbook came into effect on Monday 31 August 2026, following the all-staff consultation we ran from Monday 11 May to Friday 5 June this year. I am writing to every employee so that there is a clear written record of what changed and when it changed. Please note at the outset that this message is informational only: there is nothing you need to sign, acknowledge, complete or attend as a result of it. A copy of this notice will be held on file together with the consultation records for seven years in line with our records retention schedule.

For those who would like the detail, the significant changes are:

- Parental leave: the primary carer entitlement rises from 12 to 16 weeks and the secondary carer entitlement from 2 to 4 weeks, at full pay, for employees whose expected date of birth or placement of a child falls on or after 1 October 2026. Nobody currently on leave moves to a lower entitlement.
- Long service leave: the clauses have been rewritten to remove ambiguity about accrual during unpaid parental leave and about how continuous service is recognised following the Halden & Frey Advisory transfer of business in March 2025, consistent with the Long Service Leave Act 2018 (Vic).
- Family and domestic violence leave: the handbook now states plainly the 10 days of paid leave available each year under the National Employment Standards, that it may be taken in single days, and how to arrange it confidentially.
- Flexible working: the three interim guidelines (hybrid working, compressed weeks and purchased leave) have been consolidated into a single schedule with clearer eligibility criteria.
- Code of Conduct: restructured for readability, with a new section setting out our Positive Duty obligations under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) and a single complaint pathway replacing the two that previously operated in parallel.
- Expenses and travel: domestic per diem and kilometre rates now align with the ATO rates for the 2026-27 income year, so the handbook and the finance system no longer disagree.

Nothing in this revision reduces an existing entitlement; wherever the old handbook was more generous, the old term has been preserved.

A number of you have asked whether you need to re-acknowledge the handbook, as we asked everyone to do in 2022. You do not. The acknowledgment you signed at onboarding continues to apply through clause 4.3, and after reviewing our practice against the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) we have retired annual re-acknowledgment except where a statutory change specifically requires fresh notice. The FY26 compliance modules concluded in June and are unaffected by this revision.

The revised handbook is available on the intranet at any time under Policies & Procedures > Your Employment. I have deliberately not attached it to this message, as it runs to 84 pages and many of you print or archive these notes. If you would prefer a bound paper copy for your desk, People and Culture will arrange one - just email peopleandculture@tallowwood.com.au with your office location.
